## About this session

This is a stand-alone beginner/intermediate introduction to using the stringr package in R to manipulate text. It's pitched somewhere between a complete introduction and a more intermediate skill-builder session, so somewhere between our usual beginner (🌶) and intermediate (🌶🌶) levels. In this session:

+ we'll introduce stringr and talk about what it's for
+ we'll look at a core function toolkit
+ and we'll compare and contrast to some other ways of working with text in R
+ we **won't** try and spend a lot of time thinking about other aspects of text wrangling, or using regular expressions here as we offer other sessions designed to cover that ground

::: {.callout-tip collapse="false" appearance="default" icon="true"}
## Session resources
- [a set of words generated by blended LLM and KIND member labour](data/llm_words.xlsx), which you should download into a new Rstudio/posit project
+ you'll definitely want the [stringr cheatsheet on hand](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/strings.pdf)
:::

## Setup

Create a new project, attach the stringr and dplyr packages, load the data, and inspect:




```{.r .cell-code}
library(dplyr)
library(stringr)

words <- readxl::read_xlsx("data/llm_words.xlsx") 
```


|LLM1          |LLM2  |Human1    |Human2     |
|:-------------|:-----|:---------|:----------|
|impossible    |ouch  |Moist     |outwith    |
|paradox       |sorry |Anime     |balderdash |
|bewilderment  |home  |Eranu     |outwith    |
|serendipity   |mom   |No        |bubblegum  |
|qualia        |oops  |chocolate |I          |
|effervescence |dream |lowkey    |Marmalade  |

We'll also create a nice short vector of words to help us get up and running with our first few stringr functions:


```{.r .cell-code}
wd <- words$Human1[1:6]
```


## Detect


```{.r .cell-code}
str_detect(wd, "No") # logical output, vectorised, tells you which item contains the pattern

wd |>
  str_detect("No") # pipe-able, probably best when things get more complicated

str_which(wd, "No") # index, vectorised

str_detect(wd, "no") # case sensitive

str_detect(wd, "(?i)no") # horrid but handy

str_detect(wd, "N") # supply string or substring from anywhere in the string

str_starts(wd, "N") # find strings start that start with the pattern

str_starts(wd, "N", negate = T) # finds strings that do not start with the pattern

str_ends(wd, "o|e") # find at end, handy shorthand for several options

str_detect(wd, ".") # the pattern is really a regex - separate session!

str_count(wd, "o") # counts occurrences

str_locate(wd, "o") # note class, and beware: how many times does o occur in "chocolate"?
```

## The naming of things

+ lovely hierarchical naming convention: everything begins `str_`, and varient functions are usually named using the `_all` suffix:


```{.r .cell-code}
str_locate_all(wd, "o") # note class again
```

## A puzzle for you

Given what you already know about stringr, can you write some code to extract all and only the o-containing words from the `wd` vector please? You should return that as a new vector, containing just the o-words.


```{.r .cell-code}
wd[str_detect(wd, "o")]
wd[str_which(wd, "o")]
wd[str_detect(wd, "(?i)o")] # for the suspicious
```

## Subsetting

stringr gives you a shorthand way of doing that o-finding work:


```{.r .cell-code}
str_subset(wd, "o") # that is, it's subsetting your original vector

str_extract(wd, "o") # not very useful with the single letter

str_extract(wd, "^[A-M].*") # much more useful with regular expressions

str_extract_all(wd, "(?i)[l-n][aeiou]") # bit head-bending

str_view(wd, "(?i)[l-n][aeiou]") # might be helpful to know about

str_sub(wd, start = 1, end = 3) # by character index

str_sub(wd, start = -2) 
```

## Sorting


```{.r .cell-code}
str_sort(wd) # that returns a sorted vector
str_order(wd) # gets you the indices
```

## Lengths


```{.r .cell-code}
str_length(wd) # same as nchar(wd)

str_trunc(wd, 6)

str_trunc(wd, 6, ellipsis = "")

str_pad(wd, 9, pad = "_", side = "right") 

c("123456789", "1987654321") |> # possibly grubby way of fixing broken CHIs?
  str_pad(10, pad = "0")

c(" space before", "space afterwards ", "double  space") |>
  str_trim()

c(" space before", "space afterwards ", "double  space") |>
  str_squish()
```

## Change


```{.r .cell-code}
str_to_lower(wd)
str_to_upper(wd)
str_to_title(wd)

str_replace(wd, "o", "_")
str_replace_all(wd, "o", "_")

str_c(wd, " is ", wd) # beware lengths of vectors
str_flatten(wd, " and ")

str_glue("Nine squared is {9*9}") # basically saves you loading the glue package

words |>
  slice_sample(n = 4) |>
  str_glue_data("{LLM1} and {LLM2} are some pairs of LLM words  \n")

str_split(wd, "o") # splits at each pattern and removes it, returning a list
str_split_i(wd, "o", i = 2) # split at pattern and return ith match
str_split_fixed(wd, "o", n = 2) # splits at each match, required n as a max value. Care with the class, and examine row 5
```

There's also a weird-but-useful way of modifying substring matches. Note this will alter your `wd` vector!


```{.r .cell-code}
str_sub(wd, start = 1, end = 3) <- "clonk" # assign into substituted string
wd
wd <- words$Human1[1:6] # recreate our original vector
```
